newsitem.title: USA: Jury selection begins in U.S. Army rape case.
newsitem.headline: Jury selection begins in U.S. Army rape case.

text.p: Selection of a military jury began Tuesday in the case of Army Staff Sgt. Delmar Simpson, accused of raping six female trainees at the Army's Aberdeen Proving Ground.
Simpson, 32, is charged with 19 counts of rape and 55 other instances of sexual misconduct and other crimes while he served as a drill instructor at the proving ground beginning in 1995.
He has pleaded guilty to 16 of those counts -- 11 counts of sexual intercourse with trainees and five counts of propositioning but pleaded innocent to rape and the other charges.
On Tuesday, the military judge and attorneys for both sides began questioning the 10 potential jurors.

Questions covered issues ranging from the soldiers' exposure to media reports about the highly publicised case to their memories of their own drill instructors and whether they thought drill instructors should be held to a higher standard.

Also on Tuesday, prosecutors dropped a further 19 charges against Simpson, including charges he raped two women with whom he had pleaded guilty to having sex. Prosecutors gave no reason for the decision.
"We're surprised they actually dropped the charges," defence attorney Frank Spinner said. "It may be that the government felt that the rape allegations were weak."

Jury selection was expected to be completed Wednesday, and Simpson's court martial trial was expected to begin Friday with opening statements and initial prosecution witnesses, but it could be delayed by continued pre-trial wrangling.
The trial was expected to last two to three weeks, Army Trial Judge Col. Paul Johnston told potential jurors.
Last week, the army dropped 35 charges, including four counts of rape involving two women, and Johnston threw out 19 others.

The size of the jury has not yet been decided, although the minimum number of members was five. Simpson's lawyers have exercised their right to require that enlisted soldiers be included on the jury, meaning that at least one-third of the members must be a higher ranking non-commissioned officer than Simpson.
Pool members, chosen by base commander Maj. Gen. John Longhouser, included five enlisted soldiers and five officers -- two black men, seven white men and one white woman.

Prosecutors and defence attorneys can each strike one potential juror without cause. One of the jury pool members, a major who said his wife, a staff sergeant, had once had a professional agreement with Simpson, was excused with cause.

The Army's investigation into sexual misconduct at Aberdeen has drawn criticism that it may be racially biased, given that all 10 trainers at the base charged so far are black and most of their accusers are white. The Army has denied bias existed.

Simpson is the first of 10 soldiers charged in the military's biggest sex scandal since the 1991 Tailhook affair to go to trial, and he has been charged with the most crimes. Four other cases have been resolved through plea agreements or administrative proceedings.
